text.p: Dutch chemicals group DSM NV's polyester resins joint venture with Germany's BASF AG reflects a tough market and the logic of consolidation in the face of similar moves elsewhere, analysts said on Monday.

DSM said on Monday it had reached final agreement with BASF on a 60/40 joint venture which would be Europe's largest supplier of unsaturated polyester resins, with annual sales of around 500 million guilders.
Unsaturated polyester resins are raw materials for glassfibre-reinforced plastics, used mainly in the automotive, electrical and construction sectors.
"Every chemical company is looking for cooperation with others, that's the future," said Ab Barnevelt, analyst at Generale Bank in Rotterdam.
"Resins is a tough market, you can't really do it on your own," he said. "I think everyone is looking very hard to acquire others to help to upgrade their business to more downstream products."

DSM said the venture would focus the companies' development efforts, allowing them to serve a fragmented market constantly demanding new applications and strengthening resins against competing materials like aluminium and steel.

"By bringing together two big players and also two that are technology driven, DSM and BASF think they can really do something about the development of better applications and give the material the position it deserves," a DSM spokesman said.

"This movement to merge is something which has been going on for a long time in America and you have to be prepared. You can expect, if consolidation goes on, movement from a regional market to a global market," he said.

World production of unsaturated polyester resins totals around two million tons a year, with Europe contributing 500,000 tonnes. BASF has a nameplate capacity of 82,000 tonnes annually with DSM's nameplate capacity put at 90,000.

"This consolidation is in line with what you see in the whole industry, everybody is upgrading their portfolio," said Louise Scholtens of Gilissen Bank in Amsterdam. "Especially in polyester resins where there is some overcapacity."
"If you have overcapacity, reducing your cost base is obviously helpful."
The companies gave no details of any possible savings from the joint venture.
Barneveld said the venture was unlikely to impact significantly on DSM's bottom line as resins formed quite a minor part of the group's total activities.
"But every little helps, I suppose," he said.
In 1995, resins and plastic products contributed 79 million guilders to DSM's total operating profit of 1.52 billion. -- Andrew Clark, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
